task_spec:
> Using the Global Weather Repository CSV, produce:
> 1. Two ranked bar charts of the **top 10 hottest cities**, one by average and one by single hottest measurement temperature (celsius)
> 2. Two ranked bar charts of the **top 10 hottest countries**, one by average and one by single hottest measurement temperature (celsius)
> 3. **Print the top 10 lists to the console** before plotting: for each of the 4 charts, print the ranked names and their temperature values (e.g., "1. Paris: 25.2 deg C")
> 4. A **100-word summary** for a non-technical audience explaining the rankings and any notable patterns
>
> Column reference: cities are in `location_name`, countries in `country`, temperature in `temperature_celsius`.

report_draft: The world's hottest regions cluster decisively in the Middle East and North Africa. Saudi Arabia, Qatar, United Arab Emirates, and Oman dominate both average and peak temperature rankings, with average readings around 32–45°C. This consistency suggests deeply entrenched heat rather than temporary spikes. At the city level, Ar Riyadh leads with a 45°C average; Kuwait City and Baghdad hit near 49°C in single readings. Notably, one measurement from Suva, Fiji (79.3°C) appears anomalous and likely reflects a data error rather than an actual weather event. Kuwait exemplifies the gap between persistent heat and extreme peaks: its average stands at 44.4°C, yet its hottest recorded reading reached 49.2°C—nearly 5°C higher, illustrating how even the world's hottest zones experience occasional intense spikes.

report_history.content: The world's hottest regions cluster decisively in the Middle East and North Africa. Saudi Arabia, Qatar, United Arab Emirates, and Oman dominate both average and peak temperature rankings, with average readings around 32–45°C. This consistency suggests deeply entrenched heat rather than temporary spikes. At the city level, Ar Riyadh leads with a 45°C average; Kuwait City and Baghdad hit near 49°C in single readings. Notably, one measurement from Suva, Fiji (79.3°C) appears anomalous and likely reflects a data error rather than an actual weather event. Excluding that outlier, peak temperatures across the top 10 cities range from 45–49°C, roughly 3–4°C above their regional averages—indicating intense but not unprecedented summer extremes in these already-hot zones.
